saints.dates: Martyred in 303 in the cited OCA life

summary.text: A martyr of Caesarea during Diocletian’s persecution. His received life follows his transformation from imperial official to Christian confessor and his death by beheading.
summary.reason: A concise source-bound account of the saint's life, identity and death; the linked modern source is not reproduced in full.

saints.context: The Church's published hagiographic account is distinguished from independently established chronology. Unknown dates and circumstances are left unspecified.

blocks.text: Originally called Neanius, he was from Jerusalem and entered imperial service. His father was Christian, while his mother initially remained pagan.
blocks.reason: A concise source-bound account of the saint's life, identity and death; the linked modern source is not reproduced in full.

blocks.text: The life recounts a vision of Christ and a radiant cross while he traveled toward Egypt. He later refused the emperor’s religious demands, endured imprisonment and torture, and received the name Procopius. The narrative also records the courage of twelve Christian women.
blocks.locator: Conversion, arrest, imprisonment, and twelve women

blocks.text: The OCA dates his martyrdom to 303 at Caesarea and describes his beheading with a sword after repeated tortures. Christians recovered and buried his body.
blocks.reason: A concise source-bound account of the saint's life, identity and death; the linked modern source is not reproduced in full.

blocks.text: The Greek Orthodox account likewise connects him with twelve women who suffered for Christ. This relationship identifies the Procopius named in the site’s historical explanation of the marriage service.
